parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 18. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a bike repair shop to ask about getting two bikes serviced. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 3. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 3. Rob: Good morning, WheelWorks. Rob speaking. Anna: Oh, hello. I've got two bikes that haven't been used for a couple of years, and I'd like to get them serviced before the summer. Is that something you do? Rob: Yes, of course. That's most of our work at this time of year. Anna: They're quite different. One's a mountain bike, and the other's an ordinary road bike. They've both been in the garage since we moved house. Rob: That's fine. We service all types of bike, so that won't be a problem. Anna: Great. Is there anything I need to do before I bring them in? Rob: Well, we do ask customers to give the bikes a quick clean first, just to get the worst of the mud off. And if there are any baskets or bags attached, could you take those off, please? They tend to get in the way when we're working. Anna: OK. What about the lights? They're fixed on quite firmly. Rob: Oh, you can leave those. That's no problem. Anna: Fine. And how much does a service cost? Rob: Our standard service is sixty pounds per bike. But if you bring in two at the same time, we charge a hundred and ten altogether. Anna: That's good. Do I pay when I collect them? Rob: Yes, you pay the rest then. But we do ask for a deposit when you book, because we've had problems with people not turning up. It's just ten pounds, and it comes off the final bill. Anna: That seems fair. Rob: You can book on our website if you like, or just phone us, as you're doing now. Anna: I'll probably phone. I'm not very good with websites. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 4 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 4 to 10. Anna: So what exactly does the standard service include? Rob: Well, first we check the brakes and adjust them if necessary, and we do the same with the gears. Those are the things that usually need attention on a bike that hasn't been ridden for a while. Anna: Right. What about the tyres? I think they're completely flat. Rob: We'll pump them up, of course, and we'll tell you if they need replacing, but new tyres aren't included in the price. We'll also clean the chain and make sure it's properly oiled, because chains get very stiff if they're left for a long time. Anna: I'm sure ours have. One of the bikes was my father's, actually. It's quite old. Is that a problem? Rob: Not at all. We see lots of older bikes. We always check the frame very carefully for cracks, especially on older ones, because that can be dangerous. If we find any, we'll let you know before we do anything else. Anna: Good. Do you do anything apart from repairs? My father's bike is a horrible shade of brown. Rob: Well, we don't sell accessories, but we can have a bike painted a different colour for you. That's done by a specialist we work with, so it costs extra, and it takes about two weeks. Anna: I might think about that. My neighbour asked me to find out something, too. She's got an electric bike that keeps cutting out. Could she bring that in? Rob: I'm sorry, we can't repair electric bikes. We don't have the equipment. There's a shop in the city centre that specialises in them, though. Anna: OK, I'll tell her. And how long will a service take? Rob: It used to take about a week in the spring, because we were so busy. But we've taken on another mechanic, so now your bikes should be ready in three days. We'll send you a text message as soon as they're ready to collect. Anna: That's quicker than I expected. And where are you exactly? I've only got the phone number. Rob: We're at number forty-two Brookton Street, just behind the bus station. Anna: Could you spell that, please? Rob: Sure. It's B, R, O, O, K, T, O, N. Brookton Street. Anna: Thanks. Is there anywhere to park? Rob: There's a small car park right outside the shop, so you can unload the bikes easily. Anna: Perfect. Could I book them in for next Monday, then? Rob: Monday's fine. Just bring them in any time after half past eight. Can I take your name, please? Anna: Yes, it's Anna Webb. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a town library talking to local residents about changes at the library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Speaker: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Helen Marsh, the manager of Castlegate Library, and I'd like to tell you about some of the changes we'll be making over the next few months. But first, since many of you have asked about it, a little about the history of the building. Speaker: A lot of people assume that it was originally a school, because of the bell tower on the roof. And in the nineteen fifties, there was a plan to turn it into a hotel, although that never went ahead. In fact, it was built in eighteen ninety-five as the town's fire station. The bell was used to call the firemen when there was a fire. The fire service moved to a larger site in nineteen sixty-one, and the building has been a library ever since. If you look closely at the front of the building, you can still see where the large doors for the fire engines used to be. Speaker: Now, some of you will know the old reading room on the first floor, which hasn't been used for several years. We did consider using it for storage, and a local business offered to rent it, but in the end we decided that it should belong to the whole town. So it'll be turned into a meeting space that community groups can book free of charge. Speaker: We're also changing our opening hours. I know some of you might be worried that this is because of cuts, but in fact our funding is secure for the next three years, and we're not short of staff either. We carried out a survey last year, and a lot of residents told us they wanted to be able to use the library in the evenings, after work. So from next month, we'll stay open until eight o'clock on Tuesdays and Thursdays. On Saturdays, we'll continue to open from nine until five, as we do now. Speaker: One thing we'd like to ask you to do is to use the new self-service machines by the entrance when you borrow or return books. They're very easy to use, and it means our staff will have more time to help people with other things, such as finding information or using the computers. Speaker: And finally, many of you have asked about the café. It'll be run by an outside company, not by the library, and it should open in about three months. It'll serve light lunches as well as drinks and cakes, and there'll be some tables outside in the garden when the weather's good. You'll be glad to hear that we're relaxing the rules a little, so customers will be allowed to take hot drinks into the main library, as long as the cups have lids. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Speaker: OK, now let me tell you about the three new areas we're creating on the ground floor. Speaker: The first is the Makerspace, which will have equipment such as a 3D printer, sewing machines and basic tools. We did think about having a different theme each month, but we decided it would be more interesting to change the activities every day. So on Monday it might be 3D printing, on Tuesday sewing, and so on. There'll be a timetable on the website. Speaker: Then there's the Local History Corner. We have a lot of old photographs and documents in our collection, and we'll be putting some of these on display. The exhibitions will run for three months at a time, and we'd like local people to suggest what should go in them. So if you have ideas, or old photos of your own that you'd like to share, please tell us. Speaker: And the third area is the Quiet Room. A lot of students and people working from home have told us it's hard to concentrate in the main library, especially after school finishes. So the Quiet Room will be for adults only, and there'll be no talking or phone calls at all. Speaker: Now, a word about services. Some of the services we'll be offering are ones you'll already know about. We've been lending e-books for several years now, and our computer classes for beginners have been running for a long time. They're very popular, in fact, so do book early. And our volunteers will continue to deliver books to people who can't get to the library themselves. Speaker: But there are two services that are completely new. From September, we'll be starting language conversation groups, where people who are learning English, or any other language, can meet and practise with native speakers. And we're also launching a homework club for secondary school pupils, which will run every weekday afternoon with help from volunteer tutors. We're still looking for more tutors, so if you're a retired teacher, or you just enjoy helping young people, please do come and talk to us. Speaker: Right, if anyone has any questions, I'll be happy to answer them. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students called Emma and Josh discussing their assignment on the effect of music on studying. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Emma: So, Josh, for this assignment we have to design a study on music and learning. Have you had any ideas? Josh: Well, I usually study with music on, but I've noticed that I sometimes read the same page three times. So I've been reading about why some people find it hard to study with music on. One article said that songs with words are the real problem when you're reading, because your brain is trying to process two lots of language at the same time, the words you're reading and the words you're hearing. Emma: That makes sense. I always thought it was just that music made people tired, or that they found it annoying. Josh: So did I. But apparently instrumental music doesn't have the same effect. What do you think about the Mozart effect? You know, the idea that listening to Mozart makes you more intelligent. Emma: I read that the original study was quite small, and the improvement only lasted a few minutes. And later researchers found you got the same result with any music people enjoyed. Josh: Right. So it was probably just that the music put people in a better mood, rather than anything special about Mozart. Emma: Exactly. I think that's the most likely explanation. I'm not sure I'd want to study with Mozart anyway. Josh: Me neither. I prefer film soundtracks. They're designed not to distract you from what's happening on the screen, so maybe they work for reading too. Emma: That's an interesting thought. Oh, and did you hear about the study some students did here last year, on noise levels in the library? Josh: No. What did they find? Emma: That's the thing. They measured noise at different times of day and compared it with how much work people said they'd done, but the results were all over the place. They couldn't see any pattern at all. They did have plenty of participants, too, so it wasn't that. Josh: Hmm. Anyway, we'd better make sure we do better than last time. I got quite a low mark for my data collection. Emma: Really? That part was fine for me. My literature review was quite good too. But I lost a lot of marks on the conclusion. My tutor said it just repeated the results. Josh: Oh, that was my problem as well. I didn't really explain what the results meant. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Emma: OK, so let's plan it. Our research question could be, does background music affect reading comprehension? Josh: Good. And we'll compare three conditions: silence, instrumental music and songs with words. Emma: Right. Now, who should we use as participants? About fifteen people? Josh: That sounds about right. What about music students? Emma: I don't think so. They might start analysing the music instead of reading. What about engineering students? I know quite a few of them from my hall of residence. Josh: Good idea. Or we could ask people from the law department. Emma: I don't know anyone there. Let's stick with engineering. Josh: OK. Then for the procedure, each person reads three short passages and answers questions on them. Should we play the music through speakers? Emma: No, other noises in the room might interfere. It'd be better if they wore headphones. Then we can control the volume exactly. Josh: Right. And they can answer the questions on paper, so there are no notifications popping up on a screen. Emma: Good. And how long should each passage be? Josh: About three hundred words, I think, so that it doesn't take too long. And we should change the order of the three conditions for different people, so that they don't just get better with practice. Emma: Good point. I'll write that down. Emma: Then we'll have to deal with the ethics. We'll need every participant to sign a form giving their consent before we start. Josh: And we'll have to make sure all the data is kept anonymous. We shouldn't record anyone's name with their scores. Emma: Agreed. Then, when we've got all the results, we'll work out the average score for each condition. Josh: Should we show them in a graph? Emma: With only three conditions, I think a table would be clearer. We can put the averages and the range of scores side by side. Josh: Fine. And finally, we have to present our findings to the rest of the class in a ten-minute talk. Emma: I'm not looking forward to that part. But I think we've got a good plan. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a health sciences student giving a presentation on the health benefits of singing. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Singing is something that people in every culture do, whether it's at celebrations, at religious ceremonies or just in the shower. We usually think of it simply as a source of enjoyment. But in the last twenty years or so, researchers have started to take a serious interest in the effects of singing on our health, and what they've found is quite surprising. Student: Let's start with the effects on our mood. When we sing, the brain releases chemicals such as endorphins, which are associated with feelings of pleasure. At the same time, several studies have found that singing can lower the level of cortisol, a hormone that the body produces when we're under stress. So it's not surprising that people often say they feel calmer after singing. There's even some evidence that singing in a choir may give a small boost to the immune system, although this needs more research. Student: Singing with other people seems to have even stronger effects. In one study, researchers followed adults who had joined evening classes in either singing, creative writing or crafts. At the start, all three groups felt equally close to the others in their class. But the people in the singing classes felt closer to one another much more quickly, after just the first session. The researchers called this the ice-breaker effect. Some scientists believe that this may be one reason why singing developed in the first place, as a way of helping large groups of early humans to feel connected to one another. Student: There's also growing evidence that singing can help people with particular health conditions. For example, in the UK there are now singing groups for people with long-term lung disease. Singing teaches them to control their breathing, and many participants say that they feel less out of breath in everyday life. Singing is also being used to help people with Parkinson's disease, which often makes the voice weak and quiet. Regular singing seems to strengthen the voice, making it easier for people to be understood. Student: One study that I found particularly interesting looked at new mothers. Some women experience depression after giving birth, and in this study, mothers with symptoms of depression were divided into groups. Those who joined a singing group with their babies recovered more quickly than those who received the usual care. And the mothers said they valued the chance to do something creative that included their babies. Student: Singing seems to matter at the very beginning of life, too. Parents all over the world sing lullabies to their babies, and one study found that babies stayed calm for much longer when they heard a song than when they heard the same words spoken. Researchers think this may be because songs are slower and more repetitive than speech, which makes them easier for babies to follow. Student: What about older people? Well, one of the most moving areas of research concerns people with dementia. Even when people with dementia find it difficult to recognise their families, they can often still sing the words of songs they learned when they were young. Familiar songs can also trigger memories of events from long ago, and carers say that singing sessions can bring about a remarkable change in people's mood. Student: Singing also has social benefits for older people. Many older people live alone, and loneliness is now recognised as a serious risk to health. Studies of community choirs for older adults have found that members report much lower levels of loneliness, and many of them say that the choir has become one of the most important parts of their week. Student: There are some physical benefits too, although we shouldn't exaggerate them. Singing isn't a replacement for exercise, but it does require good posture. Choir leaders encourage singers to stand up straight, with their shoulders relaxed, so that they can breathe deeply. Over time, this can make a real difference to the way people hold their bodies. Student: So, how can people get involved? Well, choirs have become much more popular in recent years. A lot of people are nervous about joining a choir because they think they'll have to sing on their own in front of experts. But many community choirs accept anyone who wants to join. There's no audition, and you don't even need to be able to read music. Student: To sum up, the evidence suggests that singing is one of the simplest and cheapest ways to improve our mood, and it's something almost everyone can do. It doesn't require any equipment or special training, and it can be done almost anywhere. So perhaps doctors should start recommending it more often, alongside more familiar advice about diet and exercise. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a town library talking to local residents about changes at the library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Speaker: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Helen Marsh, the manager of Castlegate Library, and I'd like to tell you about some of the changes we'll be making over the next few months. But first, since many of you have asked about it, a little about the history of the building. Speaker: A lot of people assume that it was originally a school, because of the bell tower on the roof. And in the nineteen fifties, there was a plan to turn it into a hotel, although that never went ahead. In fact, it was built in eighteen ninety-five as the town's fire station. The bell was used to call the firemen when there was a fire. The fire service moved to a larger site in nineteen sixty-one, and the building has been a library ever since. If you look closely at the front of the building, you can still see where the large doors for the fire engines used to be. Speaker: Now, some of you will know the old reading room on the first floor, which hasn't been used for several years. We did consider using it for storage, and a local business offered to rent it, but in the end we decided that it should belong to the whole town. So it'll be turned into a meeting space that community groups can book free of charge. Speaker: We're also changing our opening hours. I know some of you might be worried that this is because of cuts, but in fact our funding is secure for the next three years, and we're not short of staff either. We carried out a survey last year, and a lot of residents told us they wanted to be able to use the library in the evenings, after work. So from next month, we'll stay open until eight o'clock on Tuesdays and Thursdays. On Saturdays, we'll continue to open from nine until five, as we do now. Speaker: One thing we'd like to ask you to do is to use the new self-service machines by the entrance when you borrow or return books. They're very easy to use, and it means our staff will have more time to help people with other things, such as finding information or using the computers. Speaker: And finally, many of you have asked about the café. It'll be run by an outside company, not by the library, and it should open in about three months. It'll serve light lunches as well as drinks and cakes, and there'll be some tables outside in the garden when the weather's good. You'll be glad to hear that we're relaxing the rules a little, so customers will be allowed to take hot drinks into the main library, as long as the cups have lids. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Speaker: OK, now let me tell you about the three new areas we're creating on the ground floor. Speaker: The first is the Makerspace, which will have equipment such as a 3D printer, sewing machines and basic tools. We did think about having a different theme each month, but we decided it would be more interesting to change the activities every day. So on Monday it might be 3D printing, on Tuesday sewing, and so on. There'll be a timetable on the website. Speaker: Then there's the Local History Corner. We have a lot of old photographs and documents in our collection, and we'll be putting some of these on display. The exhibitions will run for three months at a time, and we'd like local people to suggest what should go in them. So if you have ideas, or old photos of your own that you'd like to share, please tell us. Speaker: And the third area is the Quiet Room. A lot of students and people working from home have told us it's hard to concentrate in the main library, especially after school finishes. So the Quiet Room will be for adults only, and there'll be no talking or phone calls at all. Speaker: Now, a word about services. Some of the services we'll be offering are ones you'll already know about. We've been lending e-books for several years now, and our computer classes for beginners have been running for a long time. They're very popular, in fact, so do book early. And our volunteers will continue to deliver books to people who can't get to the library themselves. Speaker: But there are two services that are completely new. From September, we'll be starting language conversation groups, where people who are learning English, or any other language, can meet and practise with native speakers. And we're also launching a homework club for secondary school pupils, which will run every weekday afternoon with help from volunteer tutors. We're still looking for more tutors, so if you're a retired teacher, or you just enjoy helping young people, please do come and talk to us. Speaker: Right, if anyone has any questions, I'll be happy to answer them. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students called Emma and Josh discussing their assignment on the effect of music on studying. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Emma: So, Josh, for this assignment we have to design a study on music and learning. Have you had any ideas? Josh: Well, I usually study with music on, but I've noticed that I sometimes read the same page three times. So I've been reading about why some people find it hard to study with music on. One article said that songs with words are the real problem when you're reading, because your brain is trying to process two lots of language at the same time, the words you're reading and the words you're hearing. Emma: That makes sense. I always thought it was just that music made people tired, or that they found it annoying. Josh: So did I. But apparently instrumental music doesn't have the same effect. What do you think about the Mozart effect? You know, the idea that listening to Mozart makes you more intelligent. Emma: I read that the original study was quite small, and the improvement only lasted a few minutes. And later researchers found you got the same result with any music people enjoyed. Josh: Right. So it was probably just that the music put people in a better mood, rather than anything special about Mozart. Emma: Exactly. I think that's the most likely explanation. I'm not sure I'd want to study with Mozart anyway. Josh: Me neither. I prefer film soundtracks. They're designed not to distract you from what's happening on the screen, so maybe they work for reading too. Emma: That's an interesting thought. Oh, and did you hear about the study some students did here last year, on noise levels in the library? Josh: No. What did they find? Emma: That's the thing. They measured noise at different times of day and compared it with how much work people said they'd done, but the results were all over the place. They couldn't see any pattern at all. They did have plenty of participants, too, so it wasn't that. Josh: Hmm. Anyway, we'd better make sure we do better than last time. I got quite a low mark for my data collection. Emma: Really? That part was fine for me. My literature review was quite good too. But I lost a lot of marks on the conclusion. My tutor said it just repeated the results. Josh: Oh, that was my problem as well. I didn't really explain what the results meant. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Emma: OK, so let's plan it. Our research question could be, does background music affect reading comprehension? Josh: Good. And we'll compare three conditions: silence, instrumental music and songs with words. Emma: Right. Now, who should we use as participants? About fifteen people? Josh: That sounds about right. What about music students? Emma: I don't think so. They might start analysing the music instead of reading. What about engineering students? I know quite a few of them from my hall of residence. Josh: Good idea. Or we could ask people from the law department. Emma: I don't know anyone there. Let's stick with engineering. Josh: OK. Then for the procedure, each person reads three short passages and answers questions on them. Should we play the music through speakers? Emma: No, other noises in the room might interfere. It'd be better if they wore headphones. Then we can control the volume exactly. Josh: Right. And they can answer the questions on paper, so there are no notifications popping up on a screen. Emma: Good. And how long should each passage be? Josh: About three hundred words, I think, so that it doesn't take too long. And we should change the order of the three conditions for different people, so that they don't just get better with practice. Emma: Good point. I'll write that down. Emma: Then we'll have to deal with the ethics. We'll need every participant to sign a form giving their consent before we start. Josh: And we'll have to make sure all the data is kept anonymous. We shouldn't record anyone's name with their scores. Emma: Agreed. Then, when we've got all the results, we'll work out the average score for each condition. Josh: Should we show them in a graph? Emma: With only three conditions, I think a table would be clearer. We can put the averages and the range of scores side by side. Josh: Fine. And finally, we have to present our findings to the rest of the class in a ten-minute talk. Emma: I'm not looking forward to that part. But I think we've got a good plan. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a health sciences student giving a presentation on the health benefits of singing. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Singing is something that people in every culture do, whether it's at celebrations, at religious ceremonies or just in the shower. We usually think of it simply as a source of enjoyment. But in the last twenty years or so, researchers have started to take a serious interest in the effects of singing on our health, and what they've found is quite surprising. Student: Let's start with the effects on our mood. When we sing, the brain releases chemicals such as endorphins, which are associated with feelings of pleasure. At the same time, several studies have found that singing can lower the level of cortisol, a hormone that the body produces when we're under stress. So it's not surprising that people often say they feel calmer after singing. There's even some evidence that singing in a choir may give a small boost to the immune system, although this needs more research. Student: Singing with other people seems to have even stronger effects. In one study, researchers followed adults who had joined evening classes in either singing, creative writing or crafts. At the start, all three groups felt equally close to the others in their class. But the people in the singing classes felt closer to one another much more quickly, after just the first session. The researchers called this the ice-breaker effect. Some scientists believe that this may be one reason why singing developed in the first place, as a way of helping large groups of early humans to feel connected to one another. Student: There's also growing evidence that singing can help people with particular health conditions. For example, in the UK there are now singing groups for people with long-term lung disease. Singing teaches them to control their breathing, and many participants say that they feel less out of breath in everyday life. Singing is also being used to help people with Parkinson's disease, which often makes the voice weak and quiet. Regular singing seems to strengthen the voice, making it easier for people to be understood. Student: One study that I found particularly interesting looked at new mothers. Some women experience depression after giving birth, and in this study, mothers with symptoms of depression were divided into groups. Those who joined a singing group with their babies recovered more quickly than those who received the usual care. And the mothers said they valued the chance to do something creative that included their babies. Student: Singing seems to matter at the very beginning of life, too. Parents all over the world sing lullabies to their babies, and one study found that babies stayed calm for much longer when they heard a song than when they heard the same words spoken. Researchers think this may be because songs are slower and more repetitive than speech, which makes them easier for babies to follow. Student: What about older people? Well, one of the most moving areas of research concerns people with dementia. Even when people with dementia find it difficult to recognise their families, they can often still sing the words of songs they learned when they were young. Familiar songs can also trigger memories of events from long ago, and carers say that singing sessions can bring about a remarkable change in people's mood. Student: Singing also has social benefits for older people. Many older people live alone, and loneliness is now recognised as a serious risk to health. Studies of community choirs for older adults have found that members report much lower levels of loneliness, and many of them say that the choir has become one of the most important parts of their week. Student: There are some physical benefits too, although we shouldn't exaggerate them. Singing isn't a replacement for exercise, but it does require good posture. Choir leaders encourage singers to stand up straight, with their shoulders relaxed, so that they can breathe deeply. Over time, this can make a real difference to the way people hold their bodies. Student: So, how can people get involved? Well, choirs have become much more popular in recent years. A lot of people are nervous about joining a choir because they think they'll have to sing on their own in front of experts. But many community choirs accept anyone who wants to join. There's no audition, and you don't even need to be able to read music. Student: To sum up, the evidence suggests that singing is one of the simplest and cheapest ways to improve our mood, and it's something almost everyone can do. It doesn't require any equipment or special training, and it can be done almost anywhere. So perhaps doctors should start recommending it more often, alongside more familiar advice about diet and exercise. That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
